newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Recovery in Australian housing seen underway.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Recovery in Australian housing seen underway.

text.p: Australia's housing sector is emerging from a slump and its improving prospects are seen as a key factor behind forecasts for stronger economic growth in 1997.
Recent data has shown that the sector troughed last year, after falling from mid-1994, and was beginning to pick up by the end of the year.
Economists said leading indicators of the sector suggest that the recovery should continue through 1997.

"Housing has clearly turned the corner and one of the important pillars of a stronger economy in 1997 is firmly cemented in place," Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) senior economist Michael Blythe said.
The latest housing sector data, released on Tuesday, showed that dwelling unit commencements rose 5.9 percent in the December quarter to 30,483 from September's 28,773.
Economists said the data did confirm the Indicative Planning Council's (IPC) January statement that housing starts appeared to have troughed in the September quarter of 1996.
The IPC is the government's housing forecaster, and has forecast 127,000 housing starts for the year to June 30 1997.

Bankers Trust Australia chief economist, and IPC member, Chris Caton said the December quarter data were consistent with a September trough, and said he was now expecting average quarterly growth in starts in 1997 of three to four percent, which could see them up over 35,000 in the December quarter.
Leading indicators of the housing sector, such as finance and building approvals, as well as improved levels of affordability, support such expectations of stronger growth.
Last week, data showed housing finance approvals had reached their highest level in January since July 1994, while January building approvals were at their highest level since May 1995.
Strength in new housing has important flow through effects to other areas of the economy, such as employment, and spending on both building materials and retail goods.
However, some Australian states were still experiencing some problems due to oversupply generated in the boom of the early 1990's. The IPC estimated an oversupply of 26,000 dwellings as at June 1996.
"You've got that sort of leaning against a strong recovery, but leaning in favour of a strong recovery now is the extraordinary improvement in affordability," Caton said.
A combination of three official interest rate cuts and two rounds of competition induced cuts since the middle of 1996 has reduced mortgage rates to their lowest levels in 25 years.

"Current levels of affordability are certainly consistent with very rapid growth rates for housing," CBA's Blythe said. While an upturn in housing was generally expected, there was some disagreement on the expected pace of growth.

While some such as CBA's Blythe saw stronger growth than the market was expecting, others said the oversupply and some sluggishness in other areas of the economy would limit the upturn. ANZ Securities chief economist Philip Graham said while Tuesday's data confirmed the view that the dwelling cycle was improving, "the pick-up is likely to be slow to begin with and will not be as strong as previous dwelling cycle upturns."
Caton said that economists tended to make two errors in forecasting housing upturns -- they forecast it a bit earlier than they eventually take place, and that the strength was underestimated.
"So although we seem to have good reasons for a moderate recovery on this occasion, if it's wrong it's because the recovery is going to be stronger than that," Caton said.
